name: Adhimooleswarar Temple, Tiruppatrurai
deity: Shiva as Adhimooleswarar (Moolanathar), with the goddess Nithyakalyani
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine beside the Kollidam, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); structural temple of the Chola period with later additions
dynasty: Chola (inscriptions of Parantaka I and later Chola kings)
summary: Adhimooleswarar is the Tevaram shrine of Tiruppatrurai, the riverside place of milk beside the Kollidam, where tradition says milk welled up of its own accord over the Shiva linga to answer the prayer of the sage Markandeya.

sections.history: Tiruppatrurai stands in the river country north of the Kaveri, on the banks of the Kollidam, a short way east of Tiruvanaikaval. It is one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams, the shrines hymned in the Tevaram by the Nayanar saints of the seventh century, and Sambandar is recorded as having sung here. The name is read as paal-thurai, the milk-place on the river bank, a memory of the miracle on which the shrine is founded. Stone inscriptions of the Chola age survive within the temple, among them records of Parantaka I and Vikrama Chola, including land grants that were cut afresh when the older engravings had worn away. The deity is called Adhimooleswarar, the Lord who is the primal root, and he has been worshipped here without interruption through the long centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple is a compact, quiet Dravidian shrine of the Chola country. The sanctum faces east and holds a self-manifested Shiva linga, the Adhimooleswarar who gives the temple its name. The goddess Nithyakalyani, who is also remembered as Mekalambika and Mohanayaki, has her own shrine facing south, a direction devotees associate with gentleness toward the fear of death. Behind the sanctum, where Shiva temples usually place Lingodbhava, stands a shrine of Sankaranarayana, the joint form of Shiva and Vishnu. The inscribed stones of the Chola period line the walls, and the setting between two rivers gives the place an unhurried, green calm.
sections.legends: Two stories gather here. In the first, a Chola king hunting in the riverside country chased a bird that vanished into a bush. He loosed an arrow after it and the arrow struck an anthill, from which milk began to flow. That night Shiva appeared to him in a dream and told him that he dwelt in the anthill, and the king raised a temple on the spot. The place took the name Pattrurai from the milk. In the second, the sage Markandeya, bound by a short life, came here to pray for more. There was no water at hand to bathe the linga, and milk rose from the head of the linga itself and anointed it. In both tellings, Shiva is the Lord who answers need before it is spoken.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri in the month of Masi, in February or March, is kept with night-long worship, and Tirukarthikai in November or December fills the temple with lamps. Arudra Darshan in Margazhi honours Shiva as the cosmic dancer, and the annual Brahmotsavam draws devotees from the surrounding villages. A special worship is offered to the goddess Nithyakalyani on every full-moon day, and Pradosham is observed each month. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tiruppatrurai is a place for slow, quiet pilgrimage. It sits away from the highway, so the visit begins with a drive or ride through fields and village lanes toward the Kollidam. Come first to the sanctum of Adhimooleswarar and let the story of the flowing milk settle, then walk to the southward shrine of Nithyakalyani, and finish at the small shrine of Sankaranarayana behind the sanctum. Devotees who come on full-moon days find the goddess worshipped with special care. Few other visitors come, and the temple keeps the stillness of a riverside sanctuary.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the temple.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is about 9 km east of Tiruvanaikaval, near Panayapuram, on the Kollidam bank in Tiruchirappalli district. Tiruchirappalli Junction is the main railway station, and Tiruchirappalli has the nearest airport. Public transport to the village is limited, so an auto-rickshaw, taxi or private vehicle from Tiruvanaikaval or Tiruchirappalli is the practical way to reach it.
